author: Astrokillah
text:
All, If it's not too much to ask, I would very much like to have Master IF (or anyone who know the answer), to kindly resolve the remaining puzzle that has plagued me and a lot of other traders on this topic of ignored level. (I have received many PM and messages over this but I do not know the answer).

Staurum has laid out his hypothesis here: readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/tra...ignored-levels#64794 But there was no confirmation of such understanding from Edge (the author of Ignored Level) and Master IF.

To make life simple, allow me to post the following diagram.

Essentially, Staurum's hypothesis is this: - C is the new swapped FL for a used-up FL-A, so we trade C - F is the new swapped FL for an ignored FL-D, we do not trade F but we trade FL-D instead.

Would really appreciate if Master IF or Edge could confirm the above hypothesis.

I can understand why Staurum has come to such a conclusion, because of the mere introduction of the 'Ignored Level' concept, if we cannot make a distinction between the strength of new swapped FL- C and FL- F, then what's the merit of differentiating ignored vs used-up level?

Thank you and best regards AK

author: Astrokillah
text:
Alirezat, you were explaining the logic behind a swapped zone, my question is specifically on making the distinction between used-up level vs ignored level. Many times, when a used-up level is broken, a new swapped FL is created, and price would bounce from this swapped FL Likewise, when an ignored level is broken, a new swapped FL will also be created, and price would also bounce from this swapped FL.

So if we are to trade both scenarios the same way, i.e. either take the trade at the new swapped FL (FL-C or FL-F), or at the broken level (FL-A or D), then why pay so much attention to whether the level is ignored or not ignored?

cheers Astro

author: Rinehart
text:
I look forward to hearing from the Masters but my opinion is the reaction from D's failing to reach E creates a brand new pocket of IT orders. We know there are orders down at B (or E). When price revisits a little deeper into B in the first chart, it is reacting from the orders in that zone and that zone proves to have enough demand to break FL A.

With the second chart, D's reaction does not make it down to E yet price is able to break FL D. This tell me (perhaps incorrectly) that IT hit the buy button inside this reaction to break D. Because the move was strong enough to break D, we know there are leftover orders at this new Decision Point. This DP also sets up a really good FO zone to trick retail. I think the leftover orders and of course the ability to catch retail stops is what makes price go deeper than FL F.
